source: Shenhav, Botvinick, Cohen (2013) The expected value of control: an integrative theory of anterior cingulate cortex function
finding: Core theory. A control signal has an identity (which task or parameter) and an intensity (how hard). The brain scores each candidate signal by expected payoff minus intrinsic cost and picks the best. dACC does monitoring and this specification step. Lateral PFC does the regulation (carrying it out).
numbers: Eq.1: EVC(signal,state) = sum_i Pr(outcome_i | signal,state) * Value(outcome_i) - Cost(signal). Eq.3: signal* = argmax_i EVC(signal_i,state). Cost is a monotonic function of intensity.
quote: EVC represents the net value associated with allocating control to a given task.
limits: A conceptual theory with no new dataset in this paper. The mapping of specification to dACC is contested (see a11).
agent_relevance: Direct template for S0 and G11/G12: choose whether, which and how much to think by net value. Keep three jobs apart: monitor, decide, execute. The decider should be program code, not the model.

source: Shenhav, Botvinick, Cohen (2013) The expected value of control: an integrative theory of anterior cingulate cortex function
finding: Value is recursive. The value of an outcome is its immediate reward plus the discounted best EVC available from the next state. So today's control choice accounts for future control choices.
numbers: Eq.2: Value(outcome) = ImmediateReward(outcome) + gamma * max_i EVC(signal_i, outcome), gamma between 0 and 1.
limits: Recursion is stated but the paper gives no worked solver. Later work (Lieder 2018, a05) turns it into a learnable meta-level MDP.
agent_relevance: Gives a principled way to value a thinking step by what it unlocks later (a check now that enables a cheaper decision later), not only by its immediate payoff.

source: Shenhav, Botvinick, Cohen (2013) The expected value of control: an integrative theory of anterior cingulate cortex function
finding: Predicted shifts in intensity. A higher incentive raises the payoff curve and moves the optimal intensity up. A harder task lowers the payoff for a given intensity and moves the optimum. Supporting dACC data come from Kouneiher et al. (2009): activity rose with block incentive level, including on trials without a bonus, and with trial difficulty.
numbers: Fig.4A-B of the review: payoff curve rises with intensity, cost curve rises faster at high intensity, EVC peaks in between. Kouneiher numbers are not given in the review text.
limits: Kouneiher data are second-hand (a21). Intensity can fall again when a task is too hard to be helped by effort.
agent_relevance: Spend more tokens when payoff is high and effort helps. Stop spending when extra thinking stops raising correctness (hopeless or already-solved items).

source: Shenhav, Botvinick, Cohen (2013) The expected value of control: an integrative theory of anterior cingulate cortex function
finding: Monitoring signals that say re-specify intensity: response conflict, delays, errors, negative feedback, pain. In the Stroop network model (Cohen 1990, Botvinick 2001) conflict is co-activation of response units and means current control is too weak.
numbers: Not numeric. Stroop colour naming vs word reading: interference appears only when the task is colour naming, because word reading is the automatic default.
limits: Conflict is only one monitoring input. The review concedes dACC activity may also reflect time-on-task (Grinband 2011); it argues against that but gives no new data.
agent_relevance: Our G1 (doubt only on a signal) matches this: raise control when a conflict-like signal appears (failed check, disagreeing attempts), not on a schedule.

source: Lieder, Shenhav, Musslick, Griffiths (2018) Rational metareasoning and the plasticity of cognitive control
finding: Learned Value of Control (LVOC). Control is a meta-level decision problem. People use reinforcement learning to predict the value of each control signal from stimulus features, then pick the signal with the best predicted value minus cost. It fits learning and transfer in one visual-attention experiment and four Stroop and Flanker experiments.
numbers: BIC (lower is better), Lin et al. 2016 visual search: LVOC 1817.8, Rescorla-Wagner 9763.2, Win-Stay-Lose-Shift 3449.9, no free parameters fitted to those data. Krebs et al. 2010 reward-Stroop: LVOC 45.3, RW 1333.9, WSLS 2454.8. Cost: cost(s,c) = omega*t + exp(a*||c|| + b), opportunity cost omega set to $8/h.
limits: Fits are to published group means from five earlier experiments, simulated, not new human data. Trial-wise control treated as independent, non-sequential.
agent_relevance: Shows EVC can run as a learned estimator of what thinking is worth, fed by cheap features of the problem. Template for a learned S0 gate trained on our own bench outcomes.

source: Lieder et al. (2018) LVOC, paradigms simulated
finding: Phenomena reproduced: people learn to attend to locations predicted by colour (Lin 2016); name incongruent word colours faster and more accurately for rewarded colours (Krebs 2010); adapt control after rewarded incongruent vs congruent trials (Braem 2012); learn that control is worth more when a feature predicts incongruence (Bugg 2008, 2011).
numbers: Model-predicted reward-driven conflict-adaptation effect grows from 0.6 ms to 8.0 ms as reward sensitivity goes from 0 to 1 (t(102)=4.77, p<0.0001). Braem et al. found human reward sensitivity correlated with the effect.
limits: Effects are a few milliseconds. The original human studies were not re-opened here.
agent_relevance: Small, learnable, cue-driven shifts in effort. A scaffold can learn that a problem type earns extra checking from experience with features, not only from a fixed rule.

source: Kool, McGuire, Rosen, Botvinick (2010) Decision making and the avoidance of cognitive demand
finding: Foundation of the cost side. Given free choice between equally paid options, people prefer the lower cognitive demand option (a deck with fewer task switches) even when told the session is fixed in length, even when it causes more errors, and even when unaware of the difference.
numbers: Exp 1 (N=43, 500 trials, 90% vs 10% task-repeat decks): mean low-demand choice 0.68 (SD 0.24); 36 of 43 (84%) chose it more, p<0.0001. Errors 1.73% vs 2.58%. 14 subjects who erred more on the low-demand deck still chose it 0.80 of the time. 12 unaware subjects chose it 0.71, p=0.02.
limits: University students. Time cost is not fully separated from effort cost in Exps 1-5; Exp 6 handles that. Exp 3 found no one with a stable high-demand preference, so earlier apparent demand seekers looked like cue or position artefacts.
agent_relevance: Evidence that an effort cost exists and sits in the choice, independent of accuracy. For an LLM the analogue is a token or step cost inside the objective, not a side constraint.

source: Kool et al. (2010) Experiments 3-6
finding: The bias generalises across demand types and survives time-efficiency controls. It shrinks when a reward for finishing quickly is added, so it is motivational and sensitive to incentives.
numbers: Exp 4 (N=16, two-digit subtraction with or without carry): low-demand rate 0.73; RT 1,207 ms vs 2,026 ms; errors 0.05 vs 0.07; Cronbach alpha 0.93 over 8 runs; 7 of 16 individually significant. Exp 3 pooled N=37 (12+25). Exp 6B (N=51; 37 paid 10 cents and 14 paid 1 cent per game): payment reduced switch avoidance vs unpaid Exp 6A (p<0.01 on the JFP difference; p<0.05 on JIP minus OIP).
limits: Exp 6B: JIP 0.32 vs OIP 0.30, not significant, so paid subjects showed no residual inefficiency. Small samples (16 to 51).
agent_relevance: Effort cost is traded against reward. A token cost should be weighed against payoff, and raising payoff per item should raise the thinking budget, as in the data.

source: Westbrook, Kester, Braver (2013) What is the subjective cost of cognitive effort? Load, trait, and aging effects revealed by economic preference
finding: Cognitive effort discounting task (COG-ED). Participants choose between repeating the 1-back for a variable small payment or a higher n-back for a fixed payment. The indifference point prices extra effort in dollars. Cost rises with load, is higher in older adults, and tracks Need for Cognition.
numbers: Exp 1: 25 young (YA) and 25 older adults (OA). Subjective value of a $2.00 offer for 4-back: 0.49 (= $0.98) for YA, 0.20 (= $0.40) for OA; extra pay needed over 1-back $1.02 YA, $1.60 OA. Load effect YA F(1,122)=103, eta2=0.46; OA F(1,72)=14, eta2=0.17, holding after controlling d' and RT. AUC predicted Need for Cognition (R2=0.10, P=0.02) and beat NASA-TLX (P=0.03 vs 0.16).
limits: Small samples. Discounting was not subtractive: a $5 offer at 3-back was worth $3.07 (decrement $1.93) while a $1 offer was worth $0.60 (decrement $0.40). A plain payoff-minus-fixed-cost model misses that.
agent_relevance: A way to price effort in money. Effort cost is not constant: it scales with stakes and load, so G11/G12 should not use a flat per-token tax.

source: Westbrook et al. (2013) Experiment 2 delay-discounting benchmark
finding: Effort discounting correlated with delay discounting and showed the same amount effect (bigger offers discounted less), supporting a common subjective-value framework for effort and delay.
numbers: Exp 2: 17 YA, 16 OA (n=33). Effort AUC vs delay AUC: B=0.30, SE=0.13, P=0.03, R2=0.14. OA effort AUC was higher for $5 than $1 offers (P=0.01).
limits: R2 of 0.14 is modest. Delay choices were hypothetical; effort choices were real.
agent_relevance: Supports one cost-of-thinking currency traded against latency and tokens in the controller.

source: Shenhav, Straccia, Cohen, Botvinick (2014) Anterior cingulate engagement in a foraging context reflects choice difficulty, not foraging value
finding: A challenge to the foraging-value reading of dACC (Kolling et al. 2012). They replicated the original findings in Exp 1, then showed forage value and choice difficulty were confounded. With a corrected difficulty measure and a wider value range in Exp 2, dACC tracked choice difficulty (quadratic, not linear) and not forage value.
numbers: Exp 1: N=15, replicated all three original findings (bias to engage; dACC tracks relative forage value; dACC rises as option values converge). Exp 2 de-confounded the two: dACC showed a quadratic but not a linear relation to forage value, as the difficulty account predicts.
limits: Refutes a rival theory more than it proves EVC. EVC predicts that harder choices need more control, so it predicts the same result. It does not isolate cost-benefit computation from plain conflict or difficulty.
agent_relevance: Warning: a signal that rises with difficulty can be misread as value. Set effort from direct outcome measures (check results), not difficulty proxies.

source: Frömer, Lin, Dean Wolf, Inzlicht, Shenhav (2021) Expectations of reward and efficacy guide cognitive control allocation
finding: Tests the EVC claim that effort depends on reward and on efficacy (how much effort changes the outcome). Participants were cued with reward and with whether success depended on their performance or on a coin flip. They responded faster when reward was higher and when efficacy was higher, without losing accuracy.
numbers: Study 1 N=21: reward b=-9.81 ms, p=0.002; efficacy b=-14.9 ms, p<0.001; interaction p=0.116. Study 2 N=44 with EEG: reward b=-5.03, p=0.004; efficacy b=-5.89, p=0.016; interaction b=-9.23, p=0.009. Study 3 N=35, four levels each: reward b=-7.02, p<0.001; efficacy b=-3.85, p=0.001; interaction b=-2.27, p=0.027. Rewards $0.10 to $1.00.
limits: Effects are millisecond-scale. Study 1 interaction not significant (low power). Efficacy manipulated by coin-flip outcomes, a lab proxy.
agent_relevance: Allocate by reward times efficacy. If more thinking cannot change the answer (low efficacy), do not buy it, even when stakes are high.

source: Frömer et al. (2021) EEG results
finding: Two EEG stages. P3b (cue evaluation, about 250-550 ms) is raised by reward and by efficacy separately. The CNV (preparation before the target) is raised by both and shows their interaction, so integration appears at the control-allocation stage. Trial-by-trial amplitude predicts performance.
numbers: Study 2, N=44, 22,580 observations. P3b: efficacy b=0.44, reward b=0.34 (both p<0.001), interaction b=-0.01, p=0.948. CNV: efficacy b=-0.30 (p=0.008), reward b=-0.28 (p=0.001), interaction b=-0.35, p=0.046. Split-half r: P3b 0.86, CNV 0.75.
limits: The CNV interaction is only p=0.046. ERP source is not localised to dACC, so this does not test the dACC claim.
agent_relevance: Two stages worth separating in code: evaluate payoff and efficacy separately, then combine into one allocation decision.

source: Leng, Yee, Ritz, Shenhav (2021) Dissociable influences of reward and punishment on adaptive cognitive control
finding: Extends EVC to the form of control. With free-pace Stroop intervals, higher reward speeds responses (drift rate up) without lowering accuracy. Higher penalty for errors slows responses and raises accuracy (threshold up). The two incentives push different control parameters.
numbers: Study 1, N=32, intervals of 8-12 s, reward or penalty of $0.01 or $0.10 per trial. Reward: correct per second up (F(1,31)=28.72, p<0.001), faster RT (F(1,28)=31.83), accuracy unchanged (p=0.612). Penalty: fewer correct per second (F(1,31)=23.11, p<0.001), slower (F(1,30)=35.28), more accurate (Chisq(1)=26.73, p<0.001).
limits: Only Study 1 was read; the paper reports more studies. Reward-rate-optimal DDM is a normative benchmark, not proof of how the brain computes.
agent_relevance: Gain-framed vs loss-framed stakes change how to think (fast vs careful), not only how much. Supports letting the stake type pick the operator mix, e.g. more verification when errors are costly.

source: Vassena, Silvetti, Boehler, Achten, Fias, Verguts (2014) Overlapping neural systems represent cognitive effort and reward anticipation
finding: fMRI in mental arithmetic. Cues of upcoming high cognitive effort activated regions (ACC and striatum) that overlap with cues of high reward, supporting a shared anticipation circuit for effort and reward.
numbers: N=22. High vs low effort RT difference 760 ms; accuracy 98% vs 96% (t(21)=2.13, p=0.045). Cue pleasantness: big over small reward t(21)=9.14, low over high effort t(21)=6.87, both p<0.001.
limits: Effort cues also lowered the chance of success slightly, a confound the authors flag. Overlap is anatomical, not computational.
agent_relevance: Supports treating effort as a cost-like and anticipation-like signal handled in one system. No direct design rule.

source: Kool, Gershman, Cushman (2016) When does model-based control pay off?
finding: Boundary condition for cost-benefit arbitration. In the standard Daw two-step task and two variants, planning does not raise reward, so there is no accuracy-versus-effort trade-off to arbitrate. A redesigned task that rewards planning led humans to use more model-based control.
numbers: Simulations across learning rates and inverse temperatures: regression of reward rate on the model-based weight is near zero in the Daw, Dezfouli-Balleine and Doll tasks (small elevated region only at high inverse temperature, low learning rate, in Doll). Reward walk sigma 0.025, bounds 0.25 to 0.75, 201 trials.
limits: Human-experiment numbers were not extracted here. This shows an experimental design flaw, not a flaw in EVC.
agent_relevance: If more thinking does not improve the benchmark score, no cost-benefit controller can learn to use it. Check that extra compute pays on our tasks before trusting a learned gate.

source: Kurzban, Duckworth, Kable, Myers (2013) An opportunity cost model of subjective effort and task performance
finding: Rival cost account. Effort is felt because executive systems can serve few tasks at once, so using them carries an opportunity cost (the next-best use). Effort is the felt output of a cost-benefit computation and pushes people to reduce deployment, rather than a depleting resource.
numbers: Review, no new data. Core contrast: a computed cost, not a fuel tank running down.
limits: Review. No direct test separating opportunity-cost from intrinsic-cost forms of EVC.
agent_relevance: For an agent the cost is literal: tokens, latency and forgone parallel work. Cost should be the next-best use of the budget, not a fixed per-token fee.

source: Westbrook and Braver (2015) Cognitive effort: a neuroeconomic approach
finding: Argues effort should be defined by choice behaviour (revealed preference in effort-based decisions), not by self-report or arousal, and proposes discounting and neural value tests.
numbers: No new data. Compares neuroeconomic methods with self-report (NASA-TLX) and autonomic markers.
limits: Review. The argument rests on method fit, not on new effects.
agent_relevance: Measure what the agent chooses to spend, not what it says it spent. Log actual tokens and outcomes per item.

source: Ritz, Leng, Shenhav (2022) Cognitive control as a multivariate optimization problem
finding: Extension. Control has many degrees of freedom (threshold, drift rate, attention to target or distractor), and many settings give the same reward rate. Motor-control theory solves this with an effort cost that regularises the choice, which makes the problem well-posed.
numbers: Table 1 of the paper lists how errors, conflict and incentives change RT, drift rate and threshold in different ways. Cites a quadratic effort cost in motor control (Shadmehr, Diedrichsen) as fitting better than linear energy use.
limits: Perspective paper; the cognitive claims are proposals.
agent_relevance: With several knobs (samples, depth, checks) a cost term picks one setting. Without it, the controller has no principled way to choose among equal-accuracy settings.

source: Bustamante, Lieder, Musslick, Shenhav, Cohen (2021) Learning to overexert cognitive control in a Stroop task (as described in Ritz et al. 2022)
finding: As described by Ritz et al.: participants learned that colour naming earned more for some stimulus features, then over-used the effortful colour-naming option on a transfer test. Control biases arise from feature-specific reward learning.
numbers: No numbers read. Only the Ritz et al. 2022 description was read.
limits: Not opened (page blocked by an anti-bot check). Second-hand.
agent_relevance: Learned effort policies can over-generalise. Test the gate on unseen problem types for over-thinking.

source: Kouneiher, Charron, Koechlin (2009) Motivation and cognitive control in the human prefrontal cortex
finding: Cited by Shenhav 2013 as key dACC evidence: dACC activity increased with block incentive level (even on trials without a bonus) and with trial difficulty.
numbers: Numbers not read.
limits: Not opened. Second-hand through the review.
agent_relevance: Block-level incentive raising effort even on unrewarded items suggests a global stake level that sets a baseline budget.

source: Kolling, Behrens, Mars, Rushworth (2012) Neural mechanisms of foraging
finding: Cited by Shenhav 2013 as support: dACC tracked how much the alternative option set exceeded the current one and predicted switching. Rival reading tested by Shenhav 2014 (a11).
numbers: Numbers not read.
limits: Not opened. Contested.
agent_relevance: Leave-or-stay decisions about a line of thought may use the same value signals.

source: Kool et al. (2010) historical framing: Hull (1943) law of less work
finding: The idea that mental effort is aversive was assumed for decades without a direct test. Kool et al. say it 'appears never to have been subjected to a direct experimental test'. Decision-making precursors: Payne, Bettman and Johnson (1993) effort-accuracy trade-off in strategy choice; Smith and Walker (1993) decision-cost theory.
numbers: Historical framing only; no numbers.
limits: Historical.
agent_relevance: Payne's adaptive decision-maker is the oldest ancestor of our budget gate: pick the strategy by accuracy minus effort.

source: De Sabbata, Sumers, AlKhamissi, Bosselut, Griffiths (2024) Rational Metareasoning for Large Language Models
finding: Direct LLM use of value of computation. Reward = log p(answer | chain of thought, question) minus log p(answer | question) minus lambda times chain length. Expert Iteration trains the model to reason only when it pays. Tokens fall while accuracy holds or rises.
numbers: Averaged over datasets, Llama-3.1-8B: STaR 47.4% acc, 222.7 output tokens; RaM 50.1%, 170.8 tokens. Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct: STaR 61.9%, 215.1 tokens; RaM 63.5%, 146.2 tokens; CoT few-shot 56.4%, 253.6 tokens. Overall 23-45% fewer tokens. Out of distribution (MMLU-CF) 28-36% fewer tokens than STaR.
limits: Needs training. The utility term uses the model's own likelihood of a known target, available only at training time. Reasoning-heavy subjects (physics, engineering) saved less. Preprint.
agent_relevance: Proof of concept for EVC on LLMs and the closest match to G11/G12. We cannot train, so we need a scaffold-time proxy for the utility term (a cheap probe of agreement or check results).

source: De Sabbata et al. (2024) easy vs hard split
finding: Does the trained model adapt or just reason less? Models wrote shorter chains on items that Direct Few-Shot already solved. Plain instruct chain-of-thought did not adapt at all.
numbers: Length reduction from hard to easy split: RaM 50.3% (Llama-3.2-3B, 145 vs 72 tokens) and 36.0% (Llama-3.1-8B, 139 vs 89); STaR 34.4% and 35.9%; CoT few-shot 19.0% and 23.5%; instruct CoT prompting 0.5% and 0.9% (222 vs 221 tokens).
limits: The easy/hard split uses hindsight (whether direct answering was right).
agent_relevance: Off-the-shelf instruct models spend nearly the same tokens on easy and hard items, so an external gate has a real gap to close.

source: Lieder and Griffiths (2017) Strategy selection as rational metareasoning
finding: Precursor to LVOC (known from the 2018 paper's framing): strategy choice as maximising the value of computation.
numbers: Not read.
limits: Not opened; metadata only.
agent_relevance: Source for the formal rule: pick the strategy that maximises expected score minus time cost.

source: Musslick, Shenhav, Botvinick, Cohen (2015) A computational model of control allocation based on the expected value of control
finding: Cited by Ritz 2022 as an implementation of EVC that sets control intensity from incentives and demands.
numbers: Not read.
limits: Not opened. Web search budget was exhausted during this run and the page was not located.
agent_relevance: Would show how to build EVC in a simulated network with a fitted cost curve.

source: Callaway et al. (2022) Rational use of cognitive resources in human planning
finding: Found in a Europe PMC title search only. Not opened. No claims attributed beyond title and venue.
numbers: Not read.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Candidate for the next pass on planning-budget allocation.
